lede: The living truth of the design system was in the code; Figma was a frozen spec; and the product's AI rendered components that had never heard of the tokens. I rebuilt the foundation so all three read from the same source.

hero.figure: Pipeline diagram: DTCG token file → Figma variables → Tailwind in code → Storybook → widgets the product's AI renders. One source, three consumers.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: A B2B platform, two design systems and an AI in the middle
paragraphs: Clickmax is an all-in-one B2B platform for people who sell online: funnels, pages, products, payments, automations, all in one place, with an embedded AI assistant that answers and renders interface inside the product. I joined in January 2025 as a design system specialist, and the scope grew into product design for the platform.

When I arrived there were two design systems running in parallel: the legacy one, holding up most of the product, and a new one, incomplete and barely adopted. The living truth was in the code. Figma was a static specification, with no variables and the tokens documented as a table.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: Three consumers, no contract
paragraphs: The symptom was the usual one: designers and developers disagreeing about the right value of a spacing or a color. The cause was structural.
bullets: Figma had no Variables. Changing a token meant editing a table and hoping someone would read it.

The code had hundreds of tags for its own components plus a family of widgets for the AI assistant, none of them under contract with the design system humans used. A token change never reached what the AI rendered.
The Figma library was about 90 loose nodes on a single page, with no hierarchy, no states and no documentation.
Custom icons everywhere: 268 in use in the code, with different names and origins.
Two earlier attempts at a rebuild had stalled halfway. A third one had to prove quickly that it was different.
sections.figure: Before and after of the Figma file: the loose nodes on one page versus the library organized in 8 pages by layer.

sections.label: My role
sections.title: Architecture, decisions and building
paragraphs: I am the Senior Product Designer and Design Lead of the product, with a team of three designers. In this work I defined the token architecture, negotiated with engineering what would change and what would stay, built the foundation and the Figma library with AI assistance, and wrote the contract that defines what the product's assistant may render.

Engineering kept the stack and the code pipeline; the design team built components milestone by milestone on top of the foundation. It was the work of many people, with one rule of mine at the center: one source of truth, and only one.

sections.label: Process
sections.title: Core first, then bottom-up

steps.title: Audit
steps.text: Inventory of what existed in code and in Figma by level of composition (atoms, molecules, organisms), plus the reconciliation of the 268 icons: 233 mapped directly to an open library, 35 kept through aliases.

steps.title: Token foundation
steps.text: A first version of the DTCG file with 643 tokens; a leaner second version: 7 primitive palettes, 58 semantic tokens in two modes and 15 type scales. The semantic vocabulary became the shared lexicon of humans and AI.

steps.title: Figma variables generated from the file
steps.text: 238 variables created from the source: 132 primitive, 58 semantic and 48 component-level. Dark mode was generated by automation: 58 values, none missing.

steps.title: Bottom-up port
steps.text: Atoms, then molecules, composites and navigation, with one-to-one parity with Storybook. Button went from 7 variations to 140 (7 types × 5 sizes × 4 states) with 3 slots; Badge reached 84 variants with 49 mode-aware colors.

steps.title: Organized library
steps.text: Eight pages: 17 atoms, 47 molecules, 8 organisms, 1 template and 12 usage examples. A component is done only when it is documented.

steps.title: Human + AI contract
steps.text: The 88 tags of home-grown components were reduced to 4 families, and the family of widgets the assistant renders got a manifest: 14 widgets, all consuming the same tokens.

steps.title: Shell and visual direction
steps.text: A canonical App Shell for the new navigation and a visual direction applied to the foundation: glass surfaces in 22 places, hairlines in content, shadows only on floating surfaces.

sections.figure: Alias graph: primitive palettes → semantic tokens → component tokens, side by side in light and dark modes.

sections.label: Design decisions
sections.title: Four choices that hold up the rest

decisions.title: A neutral token layer as the single source
decisions.text: Instead of electing Figma or the code as the truth, I created a neutral layer in the DTCG format that both consume: Figma through generated variables, code through the Tailwind theme, and the AI reading the same file. After alignment with leadership, the file moved into the product's repository.

decisions.title: Change only what needs changing
decisions.text: The technical foundation of the code was good. I preserved the stack, the pipeline and the names that worked, and changed only what stood in the way of a single source. Two earlier rebuilds had died trying to redo everything.

decisions.title: A two-layer contract, led by design
decisions.text: Layer one: product components consuming tokens. Layer two: widgets the AI assistant may render, built on layer one. The AI came to be treated as one more user of the design system, under the same rules.

decisions.title: Done means documented
decisions.text: A component only counts as delivered when it is in Storybook, one-to-one with Figma, and each component lands in its own code change. It looks like bureaucracy; it is what keeps the third design system from becoming the fourth.

sections.figure: Button matrix: 7 types × 5 sizes × 4 states, with the 3 slots marked.

sections.label: Result
sections.title: What is standing today
paragraphs: The token foundation is delivered and validated, and the Figma variables are born from it, dark mode included, with no manual editing. The component library is being built milestone by milestone on that foundation, and the widget contract now defines what the product's assistant may render.

This is work in production, not a case tied with a bow. The numbers below are counts of what exists; impact measurement, such as handoff time and interface defects, comes with adoption in the code, in phases.
sections.figure: Canonical App Shell of the new navigation, with fictional data.

sections.label: Learnings
sections.title: What this work taught me
paragraphs: AI is a user of the design system too. If it renders interface, it needs the same contract a developer does, and the contract has to be in a format it can read. That changed how I write documentation: less prose, more structure.

Big things are born in Figma, small things are born in code. A color picker that took me an hour and a half in code came out in seconds in Figma; a token adjustment that would mean opening dozens of components in Figma is one line in the file. Knowing where each decision costs less is half the job.
And the usual lesson, valid for a small team as well: a design system is an agreement before it is a library.
